The Mountain swiftlet Aerodramus hirundinaceus is a small, insectivorous aerial bird endemic to the highlands of New Guinea. Field records indicate that hatchlings emerge from their nests at an extremely modest mass of just 1.1 grams [Wwb = 1.1 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available for embryonic development prior to the onset of parental provisioning. Eggs are incubated at a relatively stable 36 °C [T = 36 °C], and under these thermal conditions, the incubation period leading to hatching is approximately 24 days [ab = approximately 24 days], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other swiftlets nesting in cool montane environments. This lengthier incubation phase may be an adaptive response to the lower ambient temperatures typical of high-elevation caves and rock crevices. The slow maturation of the embryo within the calcareous shell likely serves to optimize the utilization of albumen and yolk resources, ensuring that the nestling emerges with sufficient energy reserves to withstand the brief interval before first feeding.

As the nestling chick develops under the constant attention of both parents, it undergoes a pronounced growth trajectory that culminates in a fully fledged adult body mass of approximately 10.1 grams [Wwi = approximately 10.1 grams]. This ultimate wet weight represents nearly a tenfold increase from the neonatal mass and is achieved through the regular consumption of flying insects delivered via the parents' specialized gape. Within the cave microclimate, where ambient temperatures are maintained at approximately 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] due to the metabolic heat of the colony itself, a consistent series of developmental milestones is observed. The fledgling achieves its first bout of sustained flight and leaves the nest at a remarkably early age, with the time since birth at fledging being 75 days since birth [tx = 75 days since birth] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively early fledging age is characteristic of aerodramine swiftlets and likely reflects selective pressure to minimize the period of nest vulnerability to predators such as snakes and monitor lizards.

The transition from fledgling to a fully independent juvenile is marked by a progressive reduction in parental provisioning. Juveniles hone their aerial foraging skills over several weeks, gradually shifting from a reliance on regurgitated food to capturing small dipterans and hymenopterans on the wing. The onset of gonadal maturation in this species is a comparatively slow process, driven in part by the energetic demands of building a complex, saliva-cemented nest on vertical cave walls. Under the typical thermal regime of the breeding colonies, which averages 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] owing to the substantial body heat generated by the dense aggregation of birds, the time since birth at puberty is estimated to be 225 days since birth [tp = 225 days since birth]. This protracted period of sexual development, extending across most of the first year of life, allows the young swiftlet to accumulate sufficient lipid reserves and foraging proficiency before committing to the high energetic costs of nest construction and egg production.

Upon reaching sexual maturity, the reproductively active adult engages in a highly structured breeding season that is, for montane populations of Aerodramus hirundinaceus, unusually constrained. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and rear only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], a reproductive strategy that stands in stark contrast to the multiple-brooded habits of many lowland aerial insectivores. The time since birth at first brood for this species has been documented at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], indicating that first-time breeders typically do not attempt reproduction until they are at least one year old at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This pattern of low fecundity and delayed first breeding, set against the thermal backdrop of a colony environment stabilized at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], reflects the high costs associated with constructing the durable, cup-shaped nests that are harvested by humans for bird's nest soup in some parts of the species' range.

The maximum recorded longevity for the Mountain swiftlet in the wild, based on banding studies conducted in undisturbed highland forests, reaches 10 years [am = 10 years], an exceptional lifespan for such a diminutive passerine at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This extended lifespan, which unfolds under the stable thermal conditions of the colony averaging 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], is a critical life-history adaptation that compensates for the species' markedly low annual reproductive output. With a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], this species employs a classic slow-life-history strategy typical of tropical island birds. The gradual accumulation of reproductive efforts over a decade of adult life allows a single breeding pair to potentially recruit up to ten offspring into the population over their lifetime. This demographic strategy is finely tuned to the unpredictable, insect-based food supply of montane cloud forests, where stochastic weather events can delay breeding onset and reduce chick survival in any given year.
